claim: The bacterial cell wall is essential for viability.
source: The bacterial cell wall is essential for viability, but despite its ability to withstand internal turgor must remain dynamic to permit growth and division.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell walls.

claim: Peptidoglycan is the major cell wall structural polymer.
source: Peptidoglycan is the major cell wall structural polymer, whose synthesis requires multiple interacting components.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cell wall composition.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus is a prolate spheroid that divides in three orthogonal planes.
source: The human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus is a prolate spheroid that divides in three orthogonal planes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S. aureus morphology and division pattern.

claim: Peptidoglycan synthesis occurs across the developing septal surface in a diffuse pattern.
source: Synthesis occurs across the developing septal surface in a diffuse pattern, a necessity of the observed septal geometry, that is matched by variegated division component distribution.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synthesis continues after septal annulus completion.
source: Synthesis continues after septal annulus completion, where the core division component FtsZ remains.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations.

claim: FtsZ remains at the septum after septal annulus completion.
source: Synthesis continues after septal annulus completion, where the core division component FtsZ remains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing FtsZ localization.

claim: S. aureus lacks an apparent elongasome machinery.
source: S. aureus lacks an apparent elongasome machinery, but nonetheless new peptidoglycan is inserted all over the cell surface, throughout the cell cycle, not just during cell division (Monteiro et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: New peptidoglycan is inserted all over the cell surface throughout the cell cycle in S. aureus.
source: S. aureus lacks an apparent elongasome machinery, but nonetheless new peptidoglycan is inserted all over the cell surface, throughout the cell cycle, not just during cell division (Monteiro et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: S. aureus cell volume increases at a constant rate.
source: Addition of peptidoglycan, along with its hydrolysis (Wheeler et al., 2015), is what enables S. aureus cells to get bigger – volume increases at a constant rate (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: FtsZ is an essential protein in almost all bacteria that directs cell division.
source: Chief amongst these is FtsZ - an essential protein in almost all bacteria that directs cell division, which has recently been shown to form dynamic filaments that 'treadmill' in Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis, giving a framework to assemble other division proteins resulting in cell wall biosynthesis and septum formation (Yang et al., 2017; Bisson-Filho et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FtsZ function.

claim: FtsZ forms dynamic filaments that 'treadmill' in Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis.
source: Chief amongst these is FtsZ - an essential protein in almost all bacteria that directs cell division, which has recently been shown to form dynamic filaments that 'treadmill' in Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis, giving a framework to assemble other division proteins resulting in cell wall biosynthesis and septum formation (Yang et al., 2017; Bisson-Filho et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: EzrA is a membrane protein crucial for cell division in S. aureus.
source: FtsZ assembly into the Z-ring is regulated by other cell division components including EzrA (Levin et al., 1999; Adams and Errington, 2009), a membrane protein crucial for cell division in S. aureus (Steele et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EzrA interacts with both cytoplasmic proteins and those with periplasmic domains.
source: It has been shown to interact with both cytoplasmic proteins and those with periplasmic domains and it is therefore proposed to act as an interface between FtsZ and PBPs forming a scaffold for other cell division components (Steele et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: EzrA is proposed to act as an interface between FtsZ and PBPs forming a scaffold for other cell division components.
source: It has been shown to interact with both cytoplasmic proteins and those with periplasmic domains and it is therefore proposed to act as an interface between FtsZ and PBPs forming a scaffold for other cell division components (Steele et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: EzrA exhibited punctate distribution at the division site.
source: 3D-SIM revealed that EzrA exhibited punctate distribution at the division site (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a) (Strauss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data and a citation.

claim: The mean localisation precision of eYFP calculated using the Thompson Equation was 24 (s.d. 8.5) nm.
source: The mean localisation precision of eYFP was calculated using two different formulae: the 'Thompson Equation' (Thompson et al., 2002) by the ThunderSTORM ImageJ plugin yielded 24 (s.d. 8.5) nm while a using a modified version of this equation (Mortensen et al., 2010) yielded 27 (s.d. 8.7) nm.
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data.

claim: The mean localisation precision of eYFP calculated using a modified Thompson equation was 27 (s.d. 8.7) nm.
source: The mean localisation precision of eYFP was calculated using two different formulae: the 'Thompson Equation' (Thompson et al., 2002) by the ThunderSTORM ImageJ plugin yielded 24 (s.d. 8.5) nm while a using a modified version of this equation (Mortensen et al., 2010) yielded 27 (s.d. 8.7) nm.
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data.

claim: The mean localization precision measured using NeNA analysis was 16.2 nm.
source: We also measured it experimentally using Nearest Neighbour in Adjacent Frames (NeNA) analysis (Endesfelder et al., 2014): NeNA analysis determines localisation precision based on spatial proximity of blinks that occur at similar times and is part of a family of clustering-based tools for assessing the quality of localisation microscopy data (Coltharp et al., 2012). This method gave us a mean localization precision of 16.2 nm.
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data using a specific analysis method.

claim: All of the localisations included in the analysis are within a 400 nm optical section.
source: The results were that all of the localisations included in our analysis are within a 400 nm optical section, within a range to ensure good data (Palayret et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a result from data analysis.

claim: Neither EzrA nor FtsZ are randomly distributed by angle.
source: Autocorrelation drops less quickly for EzrA and FtsZ than for simulations where angle is randomised. This shows that neither EzrA or FtsZ are randomly distributed by angle.
evidence: This is a conclusion from data analysis comparing experimental data to simulations.

claim: FtsZ and EzrA do not form a very thin ring at the leading edge of the septum in S. aureus.
source: Even with the most conservative assumptions (including simulated localisation precisions worse than we had calculated for our measured data), the localisations were spread out over a sufficiently wide range of distances to indicate that both FtsZ or EzrA do not form a very thin ring at the leading edge of the septum in S. aureus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from data analysis comparing experimental data to simulations.

claim: Both FtsZ and EzrA appear in a non-uniform distribution within the septal annulus.
source: Instead both proteins appear in a non-uniform distribution within the septal annulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from experimental observations.

claim: Within the annulus, FtsZ and EzrA show no discernible pattern within or across cells.
source: Within the annulus the proteins show no discernible pattern within or across cells.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: EzrA-meYFP foci exhibit a mixture of three different mobility components: an apparent immobile population, an intermediate mobility population, and a rapid mobility population.
source: Analysis of the mobility of tracked EzrA-meYFP foci enabled quantification of their microdiffusion coefficient (D), indicating a mixture of three different mobility components: an apparent immobile population in addition to an intermediate and a rapid mobility population (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a,b).
evidence: This is a result from single-molecule tracking analysis.

claim: The overall mean D value for EzrA foci in the septum region was 0.20 ± 0.01 μm2 s−1.
source: In total, ~600 EzrA foci tracks were analysed in the septum region, whose overall mean D value, which captures both the immobile and two mobile populations, was 0.20 ± 0.01 μm2 s−1.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: EzrA foci outside the septum region showed an increased overall mean D of 0.28 ± 0.03 µm2 s−1.
source: Whereas, 140 foci tracks were detected outside the septum region, which showed an increased overall mean D of 0.28 ± 0.03 µm2 s−1.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: The mean total copy number of EzrA molecules per cell is 305 ± 23.
source: Deconvolution analysis (Wollman and Leake, 2015) of whole cell images obtained using Slimfield microscopy indicated a mean total copy number of 305 ± 23 EzrA molecules per cell measured across a population (Figure 1—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: At least ~100 EzrA molecules per cell are not likely to be treadmilling in tight association with FtsZ.
source: Estimating the proportion of the most mobile fraction of EzrA foci therefore indicates that at least ~100 EzrA molecules per cell are not likely to be treadmilling in tight association with FtsZ.
evidence: This is an inference from the mobility data and copy number measurements.

claim: The observed mobility of EzrA cannot be accounted for by a simple treadmilling model alone in which all EzrA is tightly associated with FtsZ.
source: In other words, we cannot account for the observed mobility of EzrA by a simple treadmilling model alone in which all EzrA is tightly associated with FtsZ, rather the real cellular behaviour is more complex than this.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mobility analysis.

claim: HADA, ADA and ADA-DA mark regions of new peptidoglycan insertion.
source: We confirmed that HADA (7-hydroxycoumarin-3-carboxylic acid-amino-d-alanine), ADA (azido d-alanine) and ADA-DA (azido-d-alanyl-d-alanine) mark regions of new peptidoglycan insertion by microscopy and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data using microscopy and LC-MS.

claim: Even at 15 s labelling time, peptidoglycan synthesis was observed both at the septum and cell periphery without discrete foci.
source: Even at the very shortest labelling time (15 s) peptidoglycan synthesis was observed both at the septum and cell periphery but without discrete foci (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental imaging data.

claim: Localisation microscopy of 15 s ADA and ADA-DA labelled cells revealed labelling occurs dispersed across the whole septum as well as the off-septal cell wall.
source: Localisation microscopy of 15 s ADA and ADA-DA labelled cells revealed labelling occurs dispersed across the whole septum as well as the off-septal cell wall (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is an observation from localisation microscopy data.

claim: XY localisation precision for ADA/ADA-DA labelling was 9.9 (s.d. 3.5) nm or 7.5 nm by NeNA.
source: XY localisation precision (estimated by the Nikon N-STORM software) was 9.9 (s.d. 3.5) nm or 7.5 nm by NeNA (Endesfelder et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data.

claim: A similar pattern of peptidoglycan synthesis was seen with up to 5 min labelling with ADA or ADA-DA as a zone across the developing septum as well as throughout the off-septal cell wall.
source: A similar pattern of peptidoglycan synthesis was seen with up to 5 min labelling with ADA or ADA-DA as a zone across the developing septum as well as throughout the off-septal cell wall (Figure 3b,c,d).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental imaging data.

claim: In cells with an incomplete septum, there was a 'gap' in peptidoglycan synthesis at the mother cell wall-septum interface.
source: In cells with an incomplete septum, there was a 'gap' in peptidoglycan synthesis at the mother cell wall-septum interface (Figure 3c–i, arrows).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data.

claim: The 'gap' regions that do not contain ADA-DA are filled with peptidoglycan as shown by vancomycin binding.
source: Our two colour images show that the 'gap' regions that do not contain ADA-DA (5 min labelling), are nonetheless bound by vancomycin and thus are filled with peptidoglycan (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a conclusion from two-colour imaging data.

claim: Cells with a filled septal annulus showed continued insertion that could be resolved into two distinct zones, one for each daughter.
source: Also, cells with a filled septal annulus showed continued insertion that could be resolved into two distinct zones, one for each daughter (Figure 3c–ii).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data.

claim: PC190723 prevents depolymerisation of FtsZ and consequently inhibits cell division, leading to swollen S. aureus cells.
source: The FtsZ inhibitor PC190723 prevents depolymerisation of FtsZ and consequently inhibits cell division, also leading to swollen S. aureus cells (Haydon et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PC190723 treatment led to delocalization of peptidoglycan biosynthesis, EzrA and FtsZ even before substantial cell swelling.
source: PC190723 treatment led to delocalization of peptidoglycan biosynthesis, EzrA and FtsZ even before substantial cell swelling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Peptidoglycan synthesis was observed around the cell periphery and in distinct foci in the same place as EzrA and FtsZ after PC190723 treatment.
source: Peptidoglycan synthesis was observed around the cell periphery and in distinct foci in the same place as EzrA and FtsZ.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Non-uniform peptidoglycan insertion after PC190723 treatment results in misshapen cells with irregular thickening of the cell wall.
source: This non-uniform peptidoglycan insertion results in misshapen cells with irregular thickening of the cell wall (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is an observation from TEM data.

claim: Peptidoglycan synthesis follows localization of FtsZ and EzrA.
source: Thus, peptidoglycan synthesis follows localization of FtsZ and EzrA.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PC190723 treatment experiments.

claim: The incomplete S. aureus septum is thinner at the leading than at the lagging edge.
source: It has been shown that the incomplete S. aureus septum is thinner at the leading than at the lagging edge (Giesbrecht et al., 1998; Matias and Beveridge, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The septum of S. aureus is thinner at the leading edge and progressively thicker towards the lagging edge until it fuses.
source: The septum of S. aureus is thinner at the leading edge and progressively thicker towards the lagging edge until it fuses, at which point it is thinner at the centre and progressively thicker towards the lagging edge until ultimately uniform thickness is established (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: This is an observation from TEM data.

claim: Septal geometry dictates that peptidoglycan insertion cannot be confined to the leading edge of the septum.
source: This dictates that peptidoglycan insertion cannot be confined to the leading edge of the septum and gives a morphological explanation for the observed peptidoglycan insertion pattern.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observed septal geometry.

claim: The available surface area for peptidoglycan insertion is always larger for the observed morphology than for a uniformly thick septum.
source: Not only is the available surface area always larger for the morphology we observe, but it increases as the septum closes (whereas with a uniformly thick septum, it decreases).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling.

claim: The available surface area for peptidoglycan insertion increases as the septum closes in the observed morphology.
source: Not only is the available surface area always larger for the morphology we observe, but it increases as the septum closes (whereas with a uniformly thick septum, it decreases).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling.

claim: The non-standard cross section of the septum in S. aureus distinguishes it from other model organisms.
source: The non-standard cross section of the septum in S. aureus distinguishes it from other model organisms (Figure 5a,b,c) and indicates that not all peptidoglycan insertion occurs at the leading edge of the septum in this species prompting the development of a new model for how peptidoglycan is synthesised during the cell cycle (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the observed septal geometry.

claim: Not all peptidoglycan insertion occurs at the leading edge of the septum in S. aureus.
source: The non-standard cross section of the septum in S. aureus distinguishes it from other model organisms (Figure 5a,b,c) and indicates that not all peptidoglycan insertion occurs at the leading edge of the septum in this species prompting the development of a new model for how peptidoglycan is synthesised during the cell cycle (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claim: The non-standard septal geometry is likely advantageous to the bacteria, enabling more biosynthetic enzymes to work on the cell wall without steric hindrance.
source: This is likely advantageous to the bacteria, enabling more biosynthetic enzymes to work on the cell wall without steric hindrance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed geometry.

claim: Even at the shortest timescales, there were no foci of peptidoglycan insertion.
source: Our novel application of localisation microscopy to DAAs revealed that even at the shortest timescales and with considerably more precision than previous studies (Monteiro et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015; Turner et al., 2010), there were no foci of peptidoglycan insertion – the diffuse pattern throughout the septum and periphery of the cell was ever-present.
evidence: This is a finding from localisation microscopy experiments.

claim: The diffuse pattern of peptidoglycan insertion throughout the septum and periphery of the cell was ever-present.
source: Our novel application of localisation microscopy to DAAs revealed that even at the shortest timescales and with considerably more precision than previous studies (Monteiro et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2015; Turner et al., 2010), there were no foci of peptidoglycan insertion – the diffuse pattern throughout the septum and periphery of the cell was ever-present.
evidence: This is a finding from localisation microscopy experiments.

claim: The distribution of peptidoglycan insertion was corroborated by the distribution of core cell division components in S. aureus.
source: This surprising finding was corroborated by the distribution of core cell division components in S. aureus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing peptidoglycan insertion patterns with protein localization.

claim: FtsZ and EzrA occur in a zone and are not limited to the leading edge of the septum.
source: Localisation microscopy of FtsZ and EzrA in the septal ring showed, like the distribution of peptidoglycan insertion, that they occurred in a zone, and were not limited to the leading edge of the septum.
evidence: This is a finding from localisation microscopy experiments.

claim: When FtsZ depolymerisation was inhibited, peptidoglycan insertion occurred in areas with large amounts of FtsZ, resulting in local thickening of the cell wall.
source: When FtsZ depolymerisation was inhibited, peptidoglycan insertion was found to occur in areas with large amounts of FtsZ, resulting in local thickening of the cell wall, suggesting all synthesis may depend on FtsZ.
evidence: This is an observation from PC190723 treatment experiments.

claim: All peptidoglycan synthesis may depend on FtsZ.
source: When FtsZ depolymerisation was inhibited, peptidoglycan insertion was found to occur in areas with large amounts of FtsZ, resulting in local thickening of the cell wall, suggesting all synthesis may depend on FtsZ.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion from the PC190723 experiments.

claim: Division-associated foci of peptidoglycan synthesis have been identified in E. coli and B. subtilis.
source: This is a different scenario to E. coli and B. subtilis, where division-associated foci of peptidoglycan synthesis have been identified (albeit without the precision of localisation microscopy) and associated with cell division components driven by treadmilling FtsZ filaments (Yang et al., 2017; Bisson-Filho et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Divisome components are not placed exclusively at the leading edge of the septum.
source: Our data show that divisome components are not placed exclusively at the leading edge of the septum, and that some individual proteins move more rapidly than others.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Some individual divisome proteins move more rapidly than others.
source: Our data show that divisome components are not placed exclusively at the leading edge of the septum, and that some individual proteins move more rapidly than others.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mobility analysis.

claim: There may be a number of essentially identical machines executing peptidoglycan insertion within a region of the septum, with exchange of machine components with a more mobile population of molecules.
source: There may, therefore, be a number of essentially identical machines executing peptidoglycan insertion within a region of the septum, with exchange of machine components with a more mobile population of molecules.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the observations.

claim: The divisome machines may be very non-uniform and can execute their tasks with a subset of the complete list of divisome proteins.
source: It could also be the case that the machines are very non-uniform and can execute their tasks with a subset of the complete list of divisome proteins and with more or less of an individual protein.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative model.

claim: Stable, stoichiometric complexes may not be present and the interactions between proteins required to make new peptidoglycan may be highly transient.
source: Alternatively, stable, stoichiometric complexes are not present and the interactions between proteins required to make new peptidoglycan are highly transient.
evidence: This is another speculative alternative model.

claim: EzrA-eYFP, EzrA-meYFP, EzrA-GFP and EzrA-SNAP complement native ezrA knock-out.
source: EzrA-eYFP, EzrA-meYFP, EzrA-GFP and EzrA-SNAP complement native ezrA knock-out in SH4388 (ezrA-eyfp ΔezrA), SH4604 (ezrA-meyfp ΔezrA), SH4640 (ezrA-gfp ΔezrA) and SH4642 (ezrA-snap ΔezrA), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mutant strains with EzrA fusions showed similar growth to the wild type strain SH1000.
source: The mutant strains (doubling time 24 min) showed similar growth to the wild type strain, SH1000 (doubling time 25 min).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data.

claim: DAA labelling was reduced in SH4425 (pbp4 mutant) compared to wild type.
source: Cell growth and GlcNAc incorporation were found to be the same as WT, however DAA labelling was reduced in SH4425 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b–d).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: No significant difference in the proportion of off-septal labelling was observed between SH1000 and SH4425 (pbp4 mutant) when labelled with ADA-DA.
source: The proportion of off-septal labelling was calculated in both SH1000 and SH4425 when labelled with ADA-DA, however no significant difference was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: This is a result from quantitative analysis of imaging data.

claim: Discrete foci of peptidoglycan insertion were not observed in the pbp4 mutant.
source: Localisation microscopy of both 15 s and 5 min labelled SH4425 showed peptidoglycan synthesis both at the septal and peripheral cell wall. Discrete foci of insertion were not observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 3f–g).
evidence: This is an observation from localisation microscopy data.

claim: Comparison of autocorrelations for SH1000 and SH4425 (pbp4 mutant) revealed no substantial differences.
source: Comparison of autocorrelations (as calculated for EzrA and FtsZ, using elliptical fits) for SH1000 and SH4425 revealed no substantial differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 3h).
evidence: This is a result from data analysis.

claim: The full width half maximum spread of peptidoglycan labelling in incomplete septa is ~230 nm.
source: The full width half maximum spread of labelling is ~230 nm.
evidence: This is a measurement from cross-sectional analysis of imaging data.

claim: HADA incorporation does not cause mislocalisation of FtsZ or EzrA.
source: Incorporation of HADA does not cause mislocalisation of FtsZ or EzrA (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, though data is not shown.
